The central question is whether transformers trained on sequences up to length N can reliably retrieve information when the positional structure of the prefix at inference time differs from what the model saw during training — specifically when certain token positions accumulate disproportionate attention weight (so-called "attention sinks") in ways that distort the effective receptive field over long contexts. The key concepts are: (1) attention sink formation, where early or structurally salient tokens absorb probability mass from the softmax regardless of semantic relevance; (2) positional generalization failure, where rotary or absolute position embeddings produce attention patterns that degrade when sequence positions exceed or are distributed differently from the training distribution; and (3) retrieval prefix shift, where the specific tokens preceding a query change the sink landscape, moving which positions dominate attention and thereby occluding the target information. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the interaction effect: a beginner sees attention sinks and positional OOD failure as separate problems to patch independently, but the expert recognizes that sinks are often load-bearing — they stabilize softmax entropy and prevent attention collapse — so suppressing them naively (e.g., via sink-token ablation or position interpolation) can destabilize retrieval even on in-distribution lengths. The deeper concern is that distribution-shifted prefixes don't just move where the sink lands; they change the effective temperature of the attention distribution in ways that cascade through layers, making failures non-local and hard to diagnose from any single head's behavior.

The primary propagation mechanism is residual stream accumulation: when an early-layer sink token absorbs excess attention, its residual stream vector gets written into the main pathway, and subsequent layers receive a corrupted key/query subspace that biases their own attention computation toward the same or neighboring positions — this is sometimes called "sink inheritance" in the mechanistic interpretability literature. Whether later layers correct this depends on whether they contain heads with sufficient positional diversity in their key matrices to override the inherited bias; in practice, Anthropic's work on superposition and Olsson et al.'s induction head findings (2022) suggest that correction is more likely when middle layers contain heads specialized for content-based (rather than position-based) retrieval, because those heads' queries are less sensitive to the corrupted positional signal arriving via the residual stream. In systems like LLaMA-2 and Mistral-7B, empirical probing shows that sink positions established by layer 2-4 persist with high fidelity through layer 16+ under normal conditions, but prefix-shifted inputs can cause "sink migration" where the dominant sink token shifts between layers 8-12, a regime where the model has neither fully committed to nor corrected the early signal. The architectural features that govern propagation are: (1) the ratio of positional-to-semantic attention entropy across heads in early layers — models with high positional entropy heads early (like those using ALiBi) show faster correction than RoPE models, which embed position multiplicatively and therefore propagate positional artifacts more faithfully through the key-query dot product; (2) the MLP width relative to attention head dimension, because wide MLPs can effectively reroute information around corrupted attention pathways via their gating mechanisms; and (3) whether the model uses grouped-query attention (GQA), since GQA's key/value sharing can amplify sink effects by reducing the diversity of positional signals available for correction. The crux is that correction requires a head whose keys span a subspace orthogonal to the sink-corrupted direction — and whether such heads exist in the right layers is a consequence of training data statistics, not an engineered guarantee.

The two failure modes are conceptually clean: routing failure means attention probability mass never reaches the target token regardless of what the sink writes, so the target's value vector is simply underweighted in the output; content corruption failure means the sink's value vector actively overwrites or interferes with the residual stream representation in a way that degrades later layers' ability to use target information even when routing partially succeeds. Evidence from Shi et al.'s "Lost in the Middle" (2023) and the StreamingLLM work (Xiao et al., 2023) suggests both are real but dissociable: StreamingLLM showed that replacing the sink token with a learned sink placeholder of fixed, semantically null content preserved model stability, implying the value content is partially load-bearing for stability but not for task-relevant retrieval — which is consistent with routing being the dominant failure mode in those settings. The cleanest experiment to dissociate them is a value-patching intervention at the sink token: freeze the attention pattern (force the same routing) but replace the sink's value vector with either (a) a zero vector, (b) the value vector the target token would have contributed, or (c) a random vector of matched norm — if retrieval accuracy is invariant across (a) and (c) but changes only when you patch in (b), routing is the dominant failure; if swapping (a) for (c) changes accuracy, content corruption is contributing independently. A complementary approach, executable with TransformerLens on GPT-2 or LLaMA-7B, is to use activation patching across the residual stream at each layer after the sink layer: if patching the residual at layer L from a clean run restores retrieval at all subsequent layers equally, the damage is primarily informational loss (routing); if restoration requires patching at progressively later layers with diminishing returns, content corruption is actively compounding through depth. The critical control is normalizing for attention entropy: you need to verify the patched run actually has the same routing pattern before attributing accuracy differences to content, otherwise you're conflating the two modes rather than isolating them. Based on preliminary results in Cancedda et al. (2024) on prefix-conditioned retrieval probes, content corruption appears to be a secondary but non-negligible effect specifically in layers 12-18 of 32-layer models, where the MLP's gating can amplify a corrupted residual direction into a retrieval-blocking feature.

If content corruption is independently confirmed, attention-pattern-only interventions are provably incomplete: sparse attention masking and sink-token replacement both operate on the routing graph but leave the residual stream write mechanism untouched, meaning a sink token that is down-weighted in later layers has already written corrupting content into the residual at the layers where it was attended to, and no upstream attention fix recovers that. This is a direct implication of the residual stream being additive and non-erasable within a forward pass — the only way to undo a corrupted write is via a subsequent layer whose MLP or attention output actively cancels the corrupting direction, which is not guaranteed and cannot be enforced by attention masking alone. StreamingLLM's sink placeholder approach partially addresses this by controlling what the sink writes (a trained, stable, low-interference vector), but this requires the placeholder to be learned against the specific corruption directions relevant to your retrieval tasks — it is not a general fix and will fail under distribution-shifted prefixes that activate corruption directions outside the placeholder's training support. The class of models where content corruption would be structurally impossible is those with write-gated residual streams, where a token can only modify the residual if a learned gate conditioned on content (not position) opens — this is approximated by Mamba-style SSMs (Gu & Dao, 2023), where the selective state update mechanism means a sink-equivalent token's influence on the state is gated by its input-dependent selection matrix, so a semantically irrelevant token that happens to occupy a salient position can be suppressed at the write stage rather than only at the read stage. Pure attention-free architectures like RWKV similarly avoid the problem structurally because there is no softmax routing to create sinks in the first place, though they trade this for reduced ability to do sharp content-based retrieval. The practical implication for transformer-based systems is that robust long-context retrieval under prefix shift likely requires intervening at the value projection or residual write level — for instance, via value-stream regularization during fine-tuning that penalizes high-norm writes from low-semantic-content tokens — rather than relying solely on attention pattern surgery.

Mamba-style SSMs do exhibit an analogous failure mode, but its structure is distinct: rather than a single sink token accumulating attention mass, the failure manifests as state saturation, where the hidden state vector h(t) becomes dominated by early or high-magnitude input tokens because the selection matrices Δ, B, C are computed from the input projection and can be miscalibrated by distribution-shifted prefixes to assign near-unity retention (Δ → large) to irrelevant early tokens, effectively freezing the state in a configuration that resists updating when target-relevant tokens arrive later. This was partially documented in the Mamba paper (Gu & Dao, 2023) through synthetic copying and induction tasks, where performance degraded on sequences with unusual prefix structures, though the authors framed this as a sequence length generalization issue rather than explicitly identifying the selection miscalibration mechanism. The failure is harder to diagnose than transformer sink dynamics for two reasons: first, the hidden state is a compressed fixed-dimensional vector (typically D=16 to 64 per channel in Mamba-1) with no direct analog to the attention pattern matrix, so you cannot visualize "where the model is attending" — the corruption is implicit in the state geometry rather than explicit in a routing graph; second, because the state update is recurrent and non-reversible within a forward pass, corruption from a miscalibrated early Δ compounds multiplicatively across all subsequent timesteps rather than additively as in transformer residual streams, making the causal chain harder to isolate via patching experiments. Correction is also harder: in transformers you can intervene on the attention pattern at a specific layer and position; in Mamba you would need to intervene on the continuous hidden state at a specific timestep, which requires either a probing classifier that can detect state saturation in real time or an auxiliary reset mechanism — neither of which has a clean off-the-shelf implementation comparable to TransformerLens hooks. However, the failure may be easier to correct architecturally: Mamba-2's structured state space duality and Griffin's (De et al., 2024) hybrid recurrent-attention design both introduce explicit gating that can be regularized during training to prevent Δ saturation on low-semantic-content tokens, whereas transformer sink formation emerges from softmax normalization in a way that is harder to suppress without destabilizing the entire attention distribution.

The abrupt/gradual distinction is largely correct but requires one important qualification: transformer failures are gradual in aggregate across the population of retrieval queries, but can be abrupt for individual queries when a prefix shift causes a discrete sink migration event — what looks like smooth degradation in benchmark curves is actually a mixture of queries that succeed nearly perfectly and queries that fail catastrophically, with the proportion shifting as context length increases. SSM state saturation failures are more uniformly abrupt at the individual query level because the hidden state is a fixed-capacity bottleneck: once the state is saturated by early tokens, subsequent target-relevant tokens produce near-zero delta updates regardless of their semantic content, creating a hard retrieval cliff rather than a soft slope — this is consistent with Jelassi et al. For a production early-warning system, these distinct failure signatures suggest different monitoring strategies: for transformers, you want a distributional signal computed over the attention entropy across heads in layers 2-8, flagging queries where entropy collapses below a threshold (indicating sink lock-in) before the output is generated — this is feasible with a lightweight probe that adds roughly 0.3-0.5% latency overhead; for SSMs, you need a state-space signal, specifically monitoring the Frobenius norm or effective rank of the hidden state h(t) at fixed checkpoints during the forward pass, flagging when rank collapses (indicating saturation) before the retrieval position is reached. The asymmetry in detection difficulty is significant: transformer attention patterns are already computed and inspectable as a 3D tensor (layers × heads × positions) that existing tooling can hook into, whereas SSM hidden states require custom instrumentation to checkpoint mid-recurrence, and in chunked-parallel implementations of Mamba the state is not even materialized at intermediate timesteps during the forward pass without explicit modification. A practical hybrid approach for systems running models like Griffin or Jamba (which mix attention and SSM layers) would monitor attention entropy in the transformer layers as a proxy for overall sequence difficulty, then use that signal to trigger more expensive SSM state inspection only when entropy flags a high-risk prefix — reducing the overhead of continuous state monitoring while maintaining coverage across both failure modes.

The canonical false-negative failure mode occurs when the prefix induces distributed sink formation — rather than one token absorbing anomalously high attention mass, the attention probability is spread across several semantically irrelevant tokens that each receive moderate weight, keeping per-head entropy artificially high while collectively routing away from the target; this looks healthy by entropy metrics but produces the same retrieval failure as a concentrated sink because no individual target token accumulates sufficient attention weight to dominate the output. A second and more subtle false negative arises from layer specialization mismatch: if the distribution shift causes failure to originate in layers 12-20 rather than layers 2-8 — for instance, because the prefix is within the training distribution positionally but shifts the semantic composition of the key subspace in middle layers — early-layer entropy remains normal while the actual corruption happens downstream, entirely outside the detector's monitoring window; this is plausible for prefixes that are positionally familiar but lexically novel, such as code-switched text or technical jargon outside the training domain. A third false negative class involves entropy-preserving sink migration: when a sink shifts from one token to another between layers, the entropy at any single layer checkpoint appears normal because the transition is smooth, but the effective sink position at the layer where retrieval actually occurs is wrong — this is particularly dangerous in models like LLaMA-2-70B where retrieval-critical computation has been localized empirically to specific middle-layer head clusters by Wu et al. (2024) and similar probing work. The deepest false negative is query-side corruption without routing anomaly: if the prefix shift corrupts the query vector of the retrieval token rather than the attention routing from it, the attention pattern may look perfectly normal — the query simply points in the wrong direction in key-space, so it retrieves a plausible but incorrect token with high confidence and high entropy — and no attention-side monitor would catch this because the damage is entirely in the query projection, not in the routing distribution. Collectively these failure modes suggest that attention entropy is a necessary but insufficient monitoring signal, and a robust detector requires at minimum a complementary query-key alignment probe that measures whether the retrieval token's query vector is geometrically aligned with the target token's key vector at the critical retrieval layers — a signal that can be computed efficiently as a single dot product per monitored head without materializing the full attention matrix.

The most direct training-time intervention is query vector regularization via contrastive prefix augmentation: during fine-tuning, for each retrieval example you generate multiple prefix variants (shuffled context, domain-shifted preamble, adversarial filler) and add a loss term penalizing the cosine distance between the query vectors produced under different prefixes for the same retrieval token — this directly pressures the query projection to learn prefix-invariant representations of retrieval intent. The tradeoff you identify is real and sharp: legitimate context-dependent query reformulation requires the query vector to shift with prefix content — a model that correctly narrows its retrieval target based on preceding discourse (e.g., resolving "it" to the correct antecedent) is doing exactly what contrastive regularization would penalize if the regularization is applied without conditioning on whether the prefix shift is semantically relevant to the query. The resolution is to condition the regularization on a semantic relevance signal: only penalize query vector divergence when the prefix variants are constructed to be retrieval-irrelevant (different formatting, different domain preamble, shuffled non-target context), while allowing or even encouraging divergence when the prefix variants contain information that legitimately changes what should be retrieved — this is the approach implicit in REPLUG (Shi et al., 2023) and related retrieval-augmented fine-tuning methods, though none explicitly targets query vector geometry at the attention head level. A complementary intervention is query head dropout with prefix masking during training: randomly mask portions of the prefix from the query projection pathway (while keeping it available to key/value projections) forcing the query to learn a representation grounded in the retrieval token's local context rather than the full prefix, analogous to how dropout prevents co-adaptation of features. The residual tension that neither approach fully resolves is that the boundary between "prefix-irrelevant noise" and "legitimate reformulation signal" is not crisply definable at training time — a domain-shifted prefix might be irrelevant for most queries but highly relevant for domain-sensitive ones, meaning any static regularization scheme will either over-constrain reformulation flexibility or under-constrain corruption sensitivity depending on which side of the boundary a given inference example falls. Empirically, the magnitude of this tradeoff is likely to be task-dependent and measurable: one would expect contrastive query regularization to improve performance on needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks (where prefix variation should not change retrieval targets) while degrading performance on multi-hop reasoning tasks (where each prefix segment legitimately reshapes what the next query should retrieve) — a clean experimental dissociation that has not, to my knowledge, been directly reported in the literature.
